title: What Is the ROI of NPS, and How Do You Prove It?
summary: The ROI of NPS comes from the fixes it points to. How to trace a theme to an operational fix, a score change and money, with a budget airline example.
body_markdown:
Every net promoter score (NPS) program eventually gets the same question from finance: what are we getting for this? The survey platform, the analysts and the quarterly readout all cost money, and the score on the slide doesn't say what it earned. Most teams struggle to answer. In an[October 2026 Kustomer survey](https://www.kustomer.com/resources/pr/kustomer-study-reveals-gap-between-belief-and-proof-in-customer-experience-revenue-impact/) of 600 US customer experience (CX) decision-makers, only 21% said they successfully prove CX's direct impact on retention.


The ROI of NPS isn't in the score. It's in the fixes the score points you to, and you prove it by tracing one chain: a theme in the comments, the operational metric behind it, the fix, the change in NPS, and the money that change is worth. Thematic supports that chain by measuring how many NPS points each theme adds or costs, and by breaking any change in the score into theme-by-theme contributions with a score change waterfall. That turns "NPS went up" into "fixing baggage handling was worth 1.6 points."


Below is what the ROI of NPS actually means, what the research says about NPS and growth, a five-step method for proving the return, and a worked example from a budget airline.


## What does "the ROI of NPS" actually mean?


NPS can mean two things: the[Net Promoter Score](https://getthematic.com/insights/ultimate-guide-to-net-promoter-score) , the number, and the Net Promoter System, the management practice Bain built around it. The distinction matters for ROI. A score on its own returns nothing. The return comes from what the business changes because of it.


So the ROI of an NPS program is the value of the decisions it drove, minus what the program costs. That value usually shows up in three places:


- **Revenue.** Customers who stop hitting a problem stay longer, buy more and recommend you.
- **Cost.** Fixing the cause of a complaint removes the calls, refunds and rework it was generating.
- **Focus.** Money that would have gone to a low-impact initiative goes to a high-impact one instead.


The third is the one teams forget to count. Choosing the right fix is a return in its own right, because the wrong one still costs the same.


## Does NPS actually predict growth?


Partly. And the careful version of that answer is more useful to a finance team than the marketing version.


Bain, which created NPS, reports that[Net Promoter Scores explained roughly 20% to 60% of the variation in organic growth rates among competitors](https://nps.bain.com/about/how-net-promoter-score-relates-to-growth/) , and that an industry's Net Promoter leader outgrew its competitors by a factor greater than two times on average. Bain also puts the[lifetime value difference between detractors and promoters at 3X to 8X](https://nps.bain.com/about/numbers-behind-the-net-promoter-system) .


Independent researchers are more cautious. Keiningham and colleagues, writing in the Journal of Marketing in July 2007, used longitudinal data from 21 firms and more than 15,500 interviews to test the claim, in a paper that[challenged the fundamentals of the loyalty metric](https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/news_and_polls/2007-12/mr071220-1.pdf) . A 2022 study in the Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science concluded that[the original premise of NPS is reasonable](https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/154989) and that the methodological concerns raised by academics are valid. A[2024 study in the International Journal of Market Research](https://digitalcommons.memphis.edu/facpub2/182) found that both satisfaction and NPS significantly predict financial performance.


The takeaway for an ROI case: a market-level correlation won't convince your CFO that your own program paid off. You need evidence from your own data.


## Where does the return on NPS actually come from?


From acting on the reasons behind the score. Bain's own guidance on the Net Promoter System is blunt:[feedback that doesn't lead to action is meaningless](https://media.bain.com/Images/LOYALTY_INSIGHTS_From_feedback_to_action.pdf) .


The reasons live in the comments, and they almost always point at something operational. J.D. Power's 2025 North America Airline Satisfaction Study found that flight delays were the most common problem passengers reported, and that customers who didn't cite a problem scored[125 points higher on trust](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250507575925/en) than those who did. A score moves when the operation behind it changes.


That's why the ROI question is really a traceability question. If you can't connect a point of NPS to the operational change that produced it, you can't price it.


## How do you prove the ROI of NPS?


Five steps, each one building the evidence the next step needs.


1. **Rank themes by impact, not volume.** The most-mentioned theme is rarely the most expensive one. Thematic's[impact score](https://getthematic.com/insights/link-feedback-themes-nps-csat-drivers) shows how much your overall score would change if every comment mentioning a theme were removed, so it weighs how badly a theme scores against how many people raise it. Start from the themes costing you the most points. ([Here's how to find what's driving your NPS](https://getthematic.com/insights/find-what-is-driving-nps-score) .)
2. **Link each theme to an operational metric its owner already tracks.** "Frustrating check-in" becomes check-in wait times and kiosk failure rates. Now the theme has an owner, a number they already report, and a reason to care.
3. **Size what's fixable and price it.** Not every complaint is in your control. Estimate the share that is, then put a value on it. One practical method: compare what detractors, passives and promoters spent in the 12 months before and after they answered the survey, which gives you a value for moving a customer up a group. You can also price a theme by the churn or the support contacts it generates. Our guides on[revenue at risk in your customer feedback](https://getthematic.com/insights/revenue-at-risk-customer-feedback) and[modeling the revenue impact of an NPS increase](https://getthematic.com/insights/roi-of-cx) cover the math.
4. **Measure the score change after the fix, theme by theme.** Thematic's score change waterfall breaks the difference between two periods into green bars for themes that raised the score and red bars for themes that lowered it, and the contributions sum to the total change. If the fix worked, the theme's drag shrinks in the next period, and you can say by how many points. ([Here's how to see which themes moved your NPS](https://getthematic.com/insights/quantify-themes-moved-nps-score) .)
5. **Report the return as a portfolio, with its evidence level.** Put CX, cost and revenue initiatives on one page, so finance sees the full return rather than one lucky fix. Label each figure with its evidence level: a[before-and-after](https://getthematic.com/insights/measure-cx-initiative-impact) is stronger than a correlation, and a controlled test is stronger still. Our guide to[proving a feedback theme drives churn](https://getthematic.com/insights/prove-feedback-theme-drives-churn) walks through those evidence levels.


## What does this look like in practice?


An Asia-Pacific low-cost airline faced a familiar tension: how to prioritize customer experience improvements while keeping fares low. It ran lean P&L and insights teams, investment was heavily biased toward cost savings, and leaders couldn't track the impact of their efforts. The insights team's real problem was making NPS mean something to two different audiences.


**For commercial teams, it put a dollar value on the score.** The team combined customer spend, lifetime value and NPS: it compared what customers spent in the 12 months before and after they responded, grouped by whether they were detractors, passives or promoters. That gave a value for moving a customer from one group to the next, which turned a point of NPS into a number commercial leaders could weigh against other investments.


**For operational teams, it tied the score to metrics they control.** The airline sent its NPS scores, customer comments and contextual metadata into Thematic, which identified the reasons behind shifts in NPS. Check-in complaints were connected to sub-themes like wait times and kiosk failures, then to the metrics airport teams already track, such as check-in wait times and kiosk failure rates. Each team got its own targets and dashboard, so it could see how its work contributed to the score.


Baggage is where the two views met. It wasn't the most frequently mentioned issue, but delayed and mishandled bags were costing about 2 NPS points on key routes, and 80% of those issues were avoidable with better systems and processes. The airline invested in those systems and NPS rose 1.6 points, which is 80% of the 2-point drag, alongside what it described as a measurable boost to revenue.


Over the program, NPS rose 13%, driven by fewer flight delays, lower cancellation rates and more reliable baggage handling. The airline now plans a balanced portfolio of cost, revenue and CX initiatives under one framework with executive buy-in. As its Insights Lead put it: "What's remarkable isn't just that we improved NPS. It's that we became more efficient in the process. Thematic helped us invest smarter, not just more."


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Quoting Bain's growth correlation as your ROI.** It describes markets, not your program. Bring your own before-and-after.
- **Ranking by mention count.** Volume tells you what's loud. Impact tells you what's costing points.
- **Stopping at the theme.** A theme without an operational metric and an owner rarely gets fixed, so it never produces a return.
- **Pricing everything a theme touches.** Count only the fixable share, and keep estimates separate from measured results.
- **Ignoring the cost side.** A fix that removes failure demand pays back even when NPS barely moves.
- **Tying NPS to bonuses before the measurement is trusted.** Incentives change how the score is collected, which undermines the ROI case. See[what happens when you tie NPS to compensation](https://getthematic.com/insights/tie-nps-to-employee-compensation) .


## A checklist for your next ROI review


1. Can you name the three themes costing you the most NPS points this quarter?
2. Does each one map to an operational metric with a named owner?
3. Do you know what share of each theme is within your control?
4. Can you show, by theme, how many points last quarter's fixes recovered?
5. Is each financial figure labeled as an estimate or a measured result?
6. Does your report include cost savings, not just revenue?


## The short answer


The ROI of NPS is the value of the fixes the score leads you to, minus the cost of the program. Prove it by ranking themes by impact, linking each to an operational metric and owner, pricing the fixable share, and measuring the change in NPS theme by theme after each fix. Thematic quantifies how many points each theme costs or recovers, so the return becomes a number finance can check. Start with your single most expensive theme this quarter.
